To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
FtsZs that are 46% to 53% identical to FtsZ can function as division proteins in E. coli, provided we replace their C-terminal tail with that from E.coli.

foreign FtsZ proteins can substitute for E. coli (Ec) FtsZ, but only if the C terminus is replaced by that of EcFtsZ, and only if certain suppressor mutations are introduced into the E. coli chromosome.
the C-terminal tail of FtsZ binds FtsA and that the FtsZ C-terminal tail is required for division by FtsZ.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of the cell division machinery and the mechanisms that allow FtsZ from divergent bacteria to function in E. coli.
understanding the mechanism of FtsZ assembly, which is essential for cell division in bacteria, and with identifying the genes involved in remodeling the cell wall.
how FtsZ as a protein can evolve to function with different division proteins and with how the division proteins can evolve to function together.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
FtsZs with 40% or more sequence identity can function for cell wall constriction in vivo.
the FtsZ protein is a conserved protein that has been conserved in all bacteria.
FtsZ is the master organizer for cell division.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the C terminus of FtsZ is the key to the mechanism of cell division in all bacteria, and the rest of the protein is highly variable in sequence.
FtsZ is a highly conserved protein, but its downstream partners are not.
the C-terminal tail of FtsZ provides the link between Z-ring assembly and the downstream peptidogrycan remodeling pathways.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the C terminus of FtsZ is not a rigid binding site for downstream proteins.

FtsZ from divergent bacteria can be functionally substituted for FtsZ in E. coli, and that this can be achieved by making only two modifications: replacing the C-terminal peptide with that from E.coli and selecting for suppressor mutations in the E.coli genome.
E. coli is a useful model for studying cell division in bacteria.
